transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Well… I guess what’s been bringing me in is that I keep getting these awful doubts that I’ve missed something important. It can be something like a number on the mortgage payment, or a clause in a client proof, or whether a door is actually latched properly. And the thing is, I’ll know I checked it — I can remember checking it sometimes — but then the thought just barges back in anyway, like, what if this is the mistake that costs you everything?

It feels so intrusive and dramatic when I say it out loud, but in the moment it doesn’t feel dramatic. It feels urgent, like I’ve overlooked the one detail that’s going to cause a disaster. I’m a graphic designer, so I’m used to checking details, but this feels different from being careful. It’s like my mind won’t accept that I’ve done enough.

When these doubts come up, do you find yourself doing something over and over — like checking, counting, or repeating a phrase in your head — to try to make sure everything’s okay or to reduce the anxiety?

Yes… yes, definitely. That’s actually the part that’s been getting really out of hand.

With work, I’ll reopen the same design files after I’ve already exported them, just to make sure I didn’t leave some wrong version of a logo or a typo in a proof. And then I’ll reread the email I sent with it — not just skim it, but read it line by line, sometimes more than once, checking the attachment name, checking the wording, checking whether I implied something I didn’t mean. It sounds so small, but it can swallow up such a ridiculous amount of time.

And with payments, I’ll check the online confirmation screen, then maybe go back and check the bank site, then look at the confirmation again. Sometimes I’ll say the figures silently in my head — like the invoice number or the payment amount — over and over until it feels… settled, I guess. That’s the only word I can think of. Not even “correct,” exactly, because I might already know it’s correct. It just doesn’t feel finished until my brain sort of lets go.

A simple invoice or a little logo revision that should take, I don’t know, twenty minutes can turn into hours. And the worst part is I can’t bill for that time, because it’s not really the client asking for revisions — it’s me reopening and rereading and checking the same things again.

When you’re going through these checks or repetitions, do you feel that not doing them would lead to something bad happening, or do you do them more out of a need to be thorough without a specific fear in mind?

It’s… it’s more than just wanting to be thorough. I mean, I do tell myself that sometimes, because that sounds more reasonable — like, “I’m just being careful, this is my job, details matter.” But when I’m actually in it, it feels like if I don’t do the check, or if I stop before it feels right, then something bad could happen.

Like with a file, I’ll think, what if I sent the wrong logo version, or what if there’s a typo sitting there and the client prints it, and then it’s my fault. So I reopen the file, and then I reopen it again, and I’ll compare things I’ve already compared. With emails, I reread them line by line, and I’m not just checking spelling — I’m checking whether I said something in a way that could be misunderstood, or whether the attachment name is right, or whether I forgot something that somehow changes everything.

And with payments it’s the same kind of thing. I’ll look at the online confirmation, then go back and check the amount, then the invoice number, and sometimes I’ll repeat the figures silently in my head until they feel… settled. That’s the best way I can describe it. It’s like the information has to land in my brain properly, or I can’t trust it.

So yes, there is a fear behind it, but it’s also this uncomfortable unfinished feeling. A simple invoice or a small logo revision can stretch into hours because I can’t seem to stop reopening, rereading, and checking — and I can’t bill for that time, because it’s not real work at that point. It’s just me trying to get my brain to let go.
Do these intrusive thoughts or doubts ever feel unwanted or out of line with how you normally think, and do they cause you a lot of distress?

Yes. Very much. They don’t feel like normal “oh, I should double-check that” thoughts. They feel like they barge in, almost against my will, even when another part of me knows I’ve already looked.

Like with the mortgage payment, I can know I entered the number and checked it, but then this awful doubt comes back: what if one digit was wrong, what if I’ve missed something important? Or with a client proof, it’ll be a clause or a tiny detail, and suddenly it feels like if I don’t catch it, everything could fall apart. Even a door not being latched properly — I’ll know I checked it, but the thought still pushes back in.

And it does feel out of proportion. I know that. I can step back and think, why am I acting like one small thing will cost me everything? But in the moment it feels so urgent and upsetting, like this could be the mistake that really matters. It’s exhausting, honestly, because it doesn’t feel like me being careful anymore. It feels like my mind just won’t leave me alone.

Do you feel that these checks or mental repetitions need to be done a certain number of times or in a specific way, and if you don’t do them that way, does it increase your anxiety or make you feel like something bad might happen?

Yes… not always a fixed number, like “I have to do it exactly seven times” or something, but it does have to be done in a certain way, if that makes sense. It has to feel complete. That’s the part that’s hard to explain without sounding ridiculous.

Like if I reopen a design file to check the logo version, I can’t just glance at it. I’ll zoom in, check the filename, check the proof, look at the placement, and then sometimes I’ll close it and immediately feel like I didn’t really absorb what I saw. So I reopen it again. And if I get interrupted, or if I feel like I rushed through it, it almost doesn’t “count,” and the anxiety comes back.

Same with emails. I’ll reread them line by line, and if my attention catches on one sentence, I’ll go back to the beginning of that section, sometimes the whole email. I’m looking at the wording, the attachment name, whether I implied something wrong. It’s not that I’ve found anything new most of the time — it’s that I don’t feel settled until I’ve gone through it in a way my brain accepts.

With payments, I’ll check the online confirmation, then the amount, then the invoice number, and sometimes I repeat the figures silently in my head. Not because the number changes, obviously, but because I’m trying to make it land properly. If I stop before that settled feeling, I get this spike of anxiety, like I’m being reckless and something bad could happen.

And that’s how something that should be quick — a simple invoice, or a small logo revision — turns into hours. Hours I can’t bill anyone for, because I’m not really doing more work. I’m just trapped in checking until it finally feels okay enough to stop.
